data.name: Syakir
data.long_meaning: One who owns or possesses. Derived from the Arabic word 'saakaara' which means 'to own, to possess'. Syakir is a name of great significance in the Islamic world, and is often given to boys as a symbol of ownership and possession of their faith, or as a reminder of the responsibility and duty that comes with owning or possessing something.
data.spiritual_meaning: A name of great spiritual significance, representing ownership and possession of one's faith and responsibilities.

data.cultural_impact: The name Syakir reflects the Islamic belief in ownership and stewardship, a concept embodied in the Quranic verse "Whatever of war-booty that fall to the lot of the Messenger shall be increased for him, and it is allocated for him, and the spoils of war shall be presently distributed among the soldiers" (Al- Anfal: 71), highlighting the idea that one's possessions and wealth are not only for personal enjoyment but also for good use and redistribution to those in need.
data.spiritual_significance: Syakir is also a reminder of the spiritual ownership and possession that comes with faith in God. Muslims believe that they are God's stewards on earth, and must use their blessings and resources to serve Him and benefit the wider community. Therefore, the name Syakir serves as a constant reminder of the responsibility and duty that comes with being a believer and owner of one's faith.

islamic_reference.note: Traditional Islamic name with deep spiritual significance in Islamic culture

historical_references.reference: Ibn Al-Jawzi records the name Syakir bin Abdillah Al-Qadri in his book 'Al-Muntizam fi Tarikh al-Hakim', mentioning him as a prominent scholar and Sufi during the reign of the Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah (996-1021 CE).

Ibn Abd al-Hadid, in his work 'Sharh Nahj al-Balaghah', cites Syakir as a notable companion and teacher of Imam Shamsuddin Al-Dhahabi (d. 1348 CE). He was a Maliki jurist and a Sufi of the Shadhili order in the time of the Mameluke Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad I (1310-1341 CE).
historical_references.context: Maliki Jurist and Sufi of the Shadhili Order, Companion and Teacher of Imam Al-Dhahabi
